subtopic_detail: man with an evening urge to move his legs relieved by walking and a low ferritin on screening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old man who cannot get to sleep. For the past year he has had a deeply unpleasant crawling sensation in both calves that builds during the evening while he sits watching television and forces him to get up and walk around. Walking relieves it completely within a minute, and it returns once he sits down again.

He is worst between about 9 pm and 1 am and says he is fine during the working day. His wife says his legs do not kick once he is asleep. He has no back pain, no radiation down the leg, and no numbness or weakness. He takes no antihistamines, antidepressants or antipsychotics and drinks two cups of coffee before midday only. On examination pedal pulses are present and symmetrical, ankle reflexes are intact, and sensation and power are normal in both legs. His ferritin is 38 mcg/L (30 to 300), haemoglobin is 142 g/L (130 to 180) and transferrin saturation is 16 per cent (16 to 45).

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical present pedal pulses, intact ankle reflexes, normal power and sensation in both lower limbs
data_table.Symptom pattern: Evening onset urge to move relieved completely by walking and returning with rest, no nocturnal limb jerking reported
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 38 mcg/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 16 per cent (16 to 45), haemoglobin 142 g/L (130 to 180), renal function and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence gabapentin at a low dose each evening and titrate the dose according to response
options.rationale: Alpha 2 delta ligands are an appropriate pharmacological first line for symptomatic restless legs and are preferred over dopamine agonists. They should follow rather than precede correction of iron deficiency, which can resolve symptoms without ongoing medication. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night for a four week period with sleep hygiene advice provided
options.rationale: A hypnotic may help him fall asleep but does nothing for the sensory urge that is driving the problem, and dependence risk in a chronic condition is substantial. Sleep hygiene alone does not address a neurological sensorimotor disorder. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence pramipexole at a low dose each evening and review his response in four weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists relieve symptoms rapidly and were long used first line, which is why this remains a common answer. Augmentation, in which symptoms intensify and spread over months to years of treatment, has moved them down the ladder behind iron repletion and alpha 2 delta ligands. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies and magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine
options.rationale: This workup targets lumbosacral radiculopathy and peripheral neuropathy, the neurological near pairs, which give dermatomal or stocking distribution sensory loss and are not relieved within a minute of walking. His neurological examination is normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement taken with vitamin C and recheck the iron studies in twelve weeks
options.rationale: The urge to move with evening predominance and complete relief by walking is restless legs syndrome, and iron status is the first modifiable factor to address. A ferritin below 75 mcg/L warrants replacement in this condition even though it lies within the standard laboratory range. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome, also called Willis Ekbom disease, is diagnosed clinically on five criteria: an urge to move the legs usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, onset or worsening during rest, relief by movement, evening or night predominance, and the absence of a better explanation such as cramps or positional discomfort. Brain iron deficiency is central to the pathophysiology even when systemic iron stores appear adequate, because iron is a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase in dopamine synthesis. This is why the treatment threshold for ferritin sits far above the usual laboratory cut off, at 75 mcg/L or a transferrin saturation below 20 per cent. Secondary causes to exclude include pregnancy, chronic kidney disease and drugs including antihistamines, antidepressants, antipsychotics and dopamine antagonist antiemetics. Where pharmacological treatment is needed after iron repletion, alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin have replaced dopamine agonists as first choice because of the risk of augmentation with long term dopaminergic treatment.
key_points: Five clinical criteria: urge, rest onset, movement relief, evening predominance, no better explanation.
Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in every patient at diagnosis.
Replace iron if ferritin is below 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation is below 20 per cent.
Alpha 2 delta ligands are now preferred over dopamine agonists for symptomatic treatment.
Review medications, since antihistamines and many psychotropics provoke the condition.
explanation.pearls: Augmentation is the specific hazard of long term dopamine agonist use in restless legs: symptoms begin earlier in the day, spread to the arms and trunk, and become more intense, and the paradox is that increasing the dose briefly helps before making it worse.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome

subtopic_detail: older woman certain that mites live in her skin who brings in skin flakes sealed in a container
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman for the fifth time in three months about insects living under her skin. She has been treated twice with topical permethrin and once with oral ivermectin by a colleague and once by a dermatologist, with no change. She has fumigated her flat twice and has thrown out her mattress.

She places a small plastic container on your desk containing skin flakes, lint and a hair, and asks you to send it to the laboratory to prove the infestation. She is entirely certain about it, says the sensation of movement is constant, and will not consider any other explanation, though she holds no other unusual beliefs and there is no persecutory theme. She lives alone, manages her finances, and scores 28 out of 30 on a standardised cognitive screen. On examination there are linear excoriations and crusted erosions on the forearms and upper back, all within reach, with no burrows in the finger webs and no rash on the trunk. Full blood examination, renal function, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and a urine drug screen are all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Linear excoriations and crusted erosions on forearms and upper back confined to areas within reach, no burrows in finger webs
data_table.Cognition: Standardised cognitive screen 28 out of 30, independent in all instrumental activities of daily living
data_table.Mental state: Fixed unshakeable belief in cutaneous infestation, no other delusions, no hallucinations in other modalities, mood euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, renal and thyroid function, vitamin B12 and urine drug screen all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her for computed tomography of the brain and a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated when a late onset psychotic presentation comes with cognitive decline, focal signs or a rapid course, so it is a reasonable instinct in a 71 year old. A score of 28 out of 30 with full independence and an eight month single themed belief does not meet that threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Examine the specimen with her, then explain there are no parasites and offer a further review
options.rationale: Direct confrontation of a fixed delusion does not shift it and typically ends the therapeutic relationship, after which the patient consults elsewhere. Examining the specimen is right; stopping at contradiction leaves the condition untreated. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Examine the specimen with her, then start low dose risperidone framed as treatment for the sensation
options.rationale: A single fixed unshakeable belief of infestation with intact cognition and no other psychotic features is delusional infestation, a somatic type delusional disorder, and antipsychotic treatment produces remission in a majority. Taking the specimen seriously and treating the distressing sensation rather than debating the belief is what secures adherence. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence sertraline for an obsessive preoccupation and arrange psychology review within a month
options.rationale: Serotonergic treatment suits the patient who acknowledges the thought may be excessive, which defines an obsessional rather than a delusional presentation. She holds the belief with complete conviction, which places it outside the range that responds to this approach. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Send the specimen for microscopy and repeat the scabies treatment with a whole household approach
options.rationale: Repeat antiparasitic treatment is the correct response to genuine scabies, the near pair, which produces burrows in the finger webs and wrists, involves household contacts and itches worst at night. Four failed courses and lesions confined to reachable skin argue against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Delusional infestation, historically called delusional parasitosis or Ekbom syndrome, is a somatic type delusional disorder in which the person holds a fixed belief that they are infested by insects, worms or fibres. It is commonest in women over the age of fifty and characteristically presents to general practice and dermatology rather than to psychiatry, often after multiple failed courses of antiparasitic treatment. The specimen sign, in which the patient brings skin debris or lint in a container as proof, is highly characteristic and should be handled respectfully rather than dismissed. Secondary causes must be excluded, including substance use particularly stimulants, hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, renal and hepatic failure, dementia and true infestation. Antipsychotic treatment, historically with pimozide and now more often with risperidone, olanzapine or aripiprazole, achieves substantial improvement in most patients, and the practical difficulty is engagement rather than efficacy, so treatment is best introduced as relief for the distressing sensation and the sleeplessness rather than as treatment for a false belief.
key_points: A single fixed somatic delusion with otherwise preserved functioning defines delusional disorder.
The specimen sign is characteristic and should be examined, not dismissed.
Exclude stimulant use, thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, organ failure and true scabies.
Excoriations confined to skin the patient can reach is a useful physical clue.
Antipsychotics are effective; engagement rather than efficacy is the limiting factor.
explanation.pearls: Offer to examine the container under the microscope with the patient present rather than sending it away, because agreeing on what can be seen together preserves the alliance long enough to introduce treatment, whereas a laboratory report saying no organisms found is invariably rejected.

subtopic_detail: man eighteen months after his wife died who sets her place at the table and cannot accept she is gone
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 67-year-old man eighteen months after his wife of forty years died of pancreatic cancer. His daughter has encouraged him to come. He tells you he still sets her place at the dinner table each evening, has not moved any of her belongings, and spends several hours most days listening to voicemail messages she left him.

He says he cannot accept that she is gone, feels that part of himself died with her, and avoids the shopping centre they used to visit because it is unbearable. He has withdrawn from the bowls club he attended for twenty years. He describes intense yearning every day rather than waves that come and go, and says life has no purpose without her. He does not feel worthless, his appetite and concentration are reasonable, and he still enjoys his grandson's visits. He denies thoughts of ending his life but says he would not mind if he did not wake up. He drinks two beers most evenings, the same as before she died, and takes no medications.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful when speaking of his wife, affect reactive to other topics, no psychomotor retardation, no guilt or worthlessness
data_table.Symptom pattern: Persistent daily intense yearning and preoccupation for eighteen months, identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders
data_table.Function: Withdrawn from bowls club and social contacts, maintains self care, shopping and finances
data_table.Risk: No active suicidal ideation or plan, passive wish not to wake, no prior attempts, protective relationship with grandson

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange admission to an older persons mental health unit for assessment of his suicide risk
options.rationale: Admission is warranted for active suicidal intent, plan or significant self neglect, none of which he has. A passive wish not to wake with preserved self care and a protective relationship does not justify removing him from his home. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant at a therapeutic dose and review his response after six weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants are the right treatment when a major depressive episode is present or develops alongside the grief, and the two frequently coexist. He lacks pervasive anhedonia, worthlessness and guilt, and antidepressants have not been shown to treat the core grief symptoms themselves. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Reassure him that this is a normal response to losing a spouse and review him in three months
options.rationale: Grief of this intensity within the first six to twelve months is indeed expected and needs no intervention, so the instinct is a sound one at an earlier stage. Persisting at this severity beyond twelve months with social withdrawal and functional loss is what defines the disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Refer him to a community bereavement support group and encourage a return to his bowls club
options.rationale: Peer support and behavioural re engagement are valuable adjuncts and should be encouraged alongside treatment, so this is the closest wrong answer. Group support alone has not been shown to alter the course of established prolonged grief disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Refer for a structured grief focused psychotherapy specifically targeting the loss
options.rationale: Persistent intense yearning with identity disruption, disbelief and avoidance that is still severe and disabling at eighteen months meets prolonged grief disorder rather than normal bereavement. Grief focused psychotherapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence and outperforms general supportive counselling. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder was added as a formal diagnosis in DSM-5-TR and in ICD-11 to identify the minority of bereaved people, of the order of seven to ten per cent, whose grief does not follow the usual trajectory towards accommodation. The diagnosis requires the death of a close person at least twelve months earlier for adults, with persistent intense yearning or preoccupation on most days, together with symptoms such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, difficulty re engaging, emotional numbness, a sense of meaninglessness or intense loneliness. Normal grief characteristically comes in waves that become less frequent and less intense with time, while prolonged grief remains constant and disabling. The major differential is a major depressive episode, in which low mood is pervasive rather than focused on the deceased and worthlessness and guilt are prominent, and the two can coexist. Grief focused psychotherapy, which combines exposure to avoided reminders with work on restoring goals and relationships, has the strongest evidence and outperforms both interpersonal psychotherapy and antidepressant treatment for the core symptoms.
key_points: The diagnosis requires at least twelve months since the death in adults.
Persistent daily yearning with identity disruption and avoidance defines the syndrome.
Normal grief comes in waves that attenuate; prolonged grief remains constant.
Depression is distinguished by pervasive low mood with worthlessness and guilt.
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressants for the core grief symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Risk factors that predict prolonged grief disorder are worth eliciting at the time of a death: an unexpected or violent death, the loss of a child or spouse, high dependency on the deceased, and a lack of social support, and their presence identifies who to review deliberately at six and twelve months.

subtopic_detail: older man with abrupt memory complaints who answers most cognitive questions by saying he does not know
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 74-year-old retired accountant brought in by his son, who is worried about dementia. The son says his father's memory problems began quite suddenly about four months ago, within weeks of the death of a close friend, and have been at much the same level since.

The patient himself is the one complaining, telling you repeatedly and with distress that his mind has gone and that he is a burden. During cognitive testing he answers I do not know to most questions with little apparent effort, but when you encourage him and give extra time he recalls two of three words and correctly names the prime minister. His son reports he has stopped going to the golf club, wakes at 4 am, has lost 5 kg and has stopped reading the newspaper he read daily for fifty years. He has never got lost driving, manages his own medications correctly, and has had no falls, hallucinations or tremor. Thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, renal function, calcium and a full blood examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia, normal gait, no focal neurological signs, no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Cognitive testing: Frequent do not know responses with minimal effort, improves with encouragement and extra time, recalls two of three words on delayed recall
data_table.Collateral: Abrupt onset four months ago after a bereavement, plateaued since, early morning waking, 5 kg weight loss, withdrawal from usual activities
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, renal function, corrected calcium and full blood examination within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for formal neuropsychological testing before starting any treatment for his low mood
options.rationale: Neuropsychological assessment is genuinely useful in ambiguous presentations and will be worth arranging if he does not improve. Performed during an untreated depressive episode it underestimates ability across every domain, so the result will be misleading. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Refer for dopamine transporter imaging with a detailed sleep history taken from his partner
options.rationale: This targets dementia with Lewy bodies, which requires fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment behaviour. He has none of those features and his examination is normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.text: Commence an antidepressant at an appropriate dose and repeat cognitive testing after twelve weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt dated onset after a loss, prominent self reported deficits, do not know answers that improve with encouragement, and biological depressive features point to the cognitive impairment of depression rather than a neurodegenerative process. Treating the depression and retesting once the mood is better is the diagnostic and therapeutic step. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Commence donepezil for probable Alzheimer disease and arrange memory clinic review in three months
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease has an insidious onset over months to years with the family rather than the patient raising the concern, and patients characteristically confabulate or minimise instead of saying they do not know. Starting a cholinesterase inhibitor now treats the wrong diagnosis and leaves the depression untreated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and refer to a cognitive disorders clinic urgently
options.rationale: Structural imaging is part of a full dementia workup and would be indicated if focal signs, an unusual age or a rapid decline were present. Referring before a trial of antidepressant treatment risks a diagnostic label being applied to a reversible state. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

explanation.summary: The cognitive impairment of depression in older people, long described as pseudodementia, produces genuine deficits in attention, processing speed and effortful recall that resolve or substantially improve when the mood disorder is treated. Several features distinguish it from a neurodegenerative dementia: the onset is relatively abrupt and can often be dated, frequently to a loss or stressor, and it plateaus rather than progressing. The patient is usually the one complaining and tends to emphasise and even exaggerate the deficits, whereas in Alzheimer disease the family raises the concern and the patient minimises it. On testing, do not know answers given with little effort that improve with encouragement contrast with the confabulation and near misses of Alzheimer disease. An adequate antidepressant trial with cognitive reassessment afterwards is both treatment and test, but these patients carry a substantially elevated risk of developing a true dementia within the following few years, so follow up must continue rather than stop at recovery.
key_points: Abrupt datable onset that plateaus, often after a loss or stressor.
The patient complains and emphasises deficits while the family is less concerned.
Do not know answers improving with encouragement, rather than confabulation.
Practical function, orientation and medication management are preserved.
Treat the depression and retest; these patients still carry an elevated future dementia risk.
explanation.pearls: Around half of older people whose cognition improves with antidepressant treatment go on to develop a true dementia within five years, so recovery is a reason to schedule annual cognitive review rather than to discharge the patient from follow up.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Dementia with Lewy bodies

subtopic_detail: man weeping uncontrollably at trivial remarks after a stroke who denies feeling sad while it happens
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68-year-old man ten weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. His wife raises that he bursts into uncontrollable sobbing several times a day, often triggered by something trivial such as a television advertisement or being greeted at the door.

The episodes last a minute or two, stop as abruptly as they begin, and he is mortified by them. He tells you clearly that he does not feel sad while it is happening and that the crying seems to come from nowhere and bears no relation to how he feels. Between episodes he says his mood is reasonable, he looks forward to his grandchildren visiting, he is engaging well with rehabilitation and is pleased with his walking progress. He sleeps well, his appetite is good and his weight is stable. He has a residual mild right arm weakness and mild expressive dysphasia. He denies any suicidal thoughts, and a cognitive screen is unremarkable for his dysphasia.

data_table.Examination: Mild right arm weakness with mild expressive dysphasia, no pseudobulbar dysarthria or dysphagia
data_table.Episode description: Abrupt stereotyped crying lasting one to two minutes, trivially triggered, terminating abruptly, several times daily
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic between episodes, reactive affect, preserved anticipatory pleasure, no guilt or worthlessness
data_table.Biological features: Sleep, appetite and weight all stable, engaging actively with rehabilitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy focused on emotion regulation strategies after stroke
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is effective for post stroke depression and anxiety and remains useful adjunctive support for the distress the episodes cause. Emotionalism is a neurological release phenomenon rather than a disorder of emotion regulation, so therapy alone does not reduce episode frequency. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Reassure the couple that this settles spontaneously and review his progress in three months
options.rationale: Emotionalism does become less frequent over the first year in many patients, so the natural history offered is broadly accurate. Several distressing episodes a day at ten weeks cause real social withdrawal, and effective treatment is available now. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor titrated to a full antidepressant dose over six weeks
options.rationale: Full antidepressant dosing and a six week horizon are what post stroke depression requires, and that is the near pair here. Emotionalism responds at lower doses within days to a fortnight, so this over treats and delays the assessment of response. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a low dose and review him in two weeks
options.rationale: Stereotyped brief crying disproportionate to and dissociated from the underlying mood is post stroke emotionalism, and serotonergic antidepressants reduce episode frequency substantially. The response is typically evident within one to two weeks and at doses below those used for depression. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Arrange urgent repeat brain imaging to exclude a new infarct in the brainstem or the pons
options.rationale: Repeat imaging is warranted for new focal deficits or a change in conscious state, neither of which is present, and his examination is stable. Emotionalism after a supratentorial stroke is a recognised consequence rather than a sign of new infarction. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: Post stroke emotionalism, also called emotional lability or pathological crying and laughing, affects roughly one in five stroke survivors in the first six months and arises from disruption of corticobulbar pathways that normally inhibit brainstem motor programmes for crying and laughing. The defining feature is the mismatch between the display and the felt emotion: episodes are abrupt, stereotyped, brief, triggered by minimal or unrelated stimuli, and the patient reports little or no corresponding sadness. This dissociation is what distinguishes it from post stroke depression, in which crying accompanies genuinely low mood, and where anhedonia, hopelessness, sleep disturbance and appetite change are also present. The two conditions frequently coexist, so both must be assessed rather than assuming one excludes the other. Serotonergic antidepressants are effective and characteristically work faster and at lower doses than in depression, and the improvement is often striking within the first fortnight; explaining the mechanism to the patient and family also substantially reduces the embarrassment and the social withdrawal that accompany it.
key_points: Abrupt stereotyped crying dissociated from the felt emotion defines emotionalism.
Post stroke depression brings pervasive low mood with anhedonia and biological features.
The two conditions commonly coexist and both must be assessed.
Serotonergic antidepressants work at lower doses and faster than in depression.
Explanation to patient and family reduces embarrassment and social withdrawal.
explanation.pearls: The speed of response is itself diagnostic: emotionalism typically improves within three to fourteen days of starting a serotonergic antidepressant, so a patient still crying unchanged at four weeks should prompt reconsideration of post stroke depression rather than a dose increase.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
